5.6.2 The Administrator of the UT of Lakshadweep informed the Committee that the Coconut & 
Fish play the most important role in the life of every citizen in Lakshadweep.  The total catch of all 
fisheries in the calendar year 2019 was 22928 tonnes (Tuna verities constituting 19444 tonnes). 
Further, the U.T. of Lakshadweep has recently issued guidelines (20 th December, 2019) for issuing 
NOC for collecting fresh fishes (Tuna & Tuna like fishes) from Lakshadweep to the mainland.   
This has enabled the Marine Products Export Devel opment Authority (MPEDA) registered 
Exporters to collect fish & allied products from Lakshadweep.  Three such exporters have visited , 
explored and send samples of fresh Tuna & Dried Tuna to Japan, Sri Lanka and USA.  One 
exporter has set-up a small office in Agatti for the purchase of Yellow Fin Tuna (much in demand 
in Japan).  Some of his international buyers have already visited the islands.  
 
5.6.3 Regarding Dried Tuna (Massmeen), the Administrator of the UT of Lakshadweep submitted 
that traditionally, the only method of preservation of tuna known to the islands is drying the same.  
The dried product is Massmeen, which is the only way of preservation for transportation and trade 
and hoarding for rainy seasons.  This primitive method of drying the fish is laborious, time -
consuming and uneconomical.  Therefore, there is a need to train them and establish centres for 
packing of fresh catch for export.  This transition may take time.  Slowly, it is proposed to phase 
out the drying method because Lakshadweep ha s modern technology that can help in exporting 
fresh tuna.  Till such time, there is a need to give a minimum support price for producing 
Massmeen (dried fish).  There is a market for the same in Japan & Sri Lanka. Besides, a Committee 
has been constituted  under the chairmanship of Secretary (Fisheries) with Member of Parliament, 
President cum Chief Counselor, District Panchayat and other officers for fixing an MSP for 
Massmeen. The above mentioned Committee has discovered that minimum cost production of 
Massmeen is Rs.456/- per kg and recommended a support price of Rs.400/- per kg.  The department 
proposes to the same and sells the product through Lakshadweep Co -operative Marketing 
Federation.  It is also proposed to give GAP funding to the Lakshadweep Co -operative Marketing 
Federation and for that, the UT of Lakshadweep may need a budget provision of Rs. 12 crore to 
support the scheme.    
 
5.6.4 The Committee takes note of the huge potential of fish production in Lakshadweep. 
The Committee, therefore, recom mends that a scientific approach for development and 
modernization of the fisheries sector in Lakshadweep may be adopted at all stages from fish 
catching and its subsequent handling to its storage, processing and packaging. The 
Committee also recommends th at better fishing equipment s and training should be provided 
to the fishermen and better deep freezing plants, canning facilities and fish processing units 
be established on a priority basis. The Committee observes that Lakshadweep has 
tremendous potential  for fish export, especially Massmeen but concrete measures are 
required to harness this potential. The Committee, in this connection, recommends that the 
Ministry along with the administration of the UT of Lakshadweep must chalk out a detailed 
strategy, i n consultation with the Marine Products Export Development Authority, for 
developing the export potential of marine produce of Lakshadweep which would improve the 
economy of Lakshadweep. The Committee further recommends the Ministry to take up the 
matter with the Ministry of Finance for allocation of a sum of Rs. 12 crore as projected by the 
UT, for procuring Massmeen at MSP on a priority basis.

5.6.6 The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in para (2.1.8) of its 204 th Report 
on Administration and Development of Union Territory of Lakshadweep that the growth of 
tourism in Lakshadweep is h ighly desirable as it would not only generate employment 
opportunities but also bring foreign exchange to Lakshadweep. However, reckless and 
unsystematic growth may prove to be counter-productive by harming the fragile ecosystem of 
the Islands. Hence, the Committee feels that the tourism plan of the UT Administration must 
strike a balance between the realization of tourism potential and the ecological sustainability 
of the Islands. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs 
must strive to develop the tourism in Lakshadweep on the development model adopted by 
Maldives and Mauritius, both of which focus on high -end and low -volume luxury tourism, 
along with continuing the current cruise -based tourism approach which would certainly he lp 
to regulate the number of visitors to the Islands and to generate substantial amount of 
revenue.

is Rs. 52863.91 that is divided in to two parts. i.e. Union Territories (without legislature) is Rs.

 National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) 
 
 The Committee observes that there is always a disparity  between the assessment of 
damage due to disaster made by the States and the assessment made by the Ministry of Home 
Affairs. The reason for the same could be that the Central study teams are sent for an 

 
 
106 
 
assessment of damages and casualties months after th e occurrence of disaster and by the time 
that teams reaches the disaster -affected area, the signs of disaster are on the verge of 
diminishing.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Study Teams should make a 
preliminary visit to the disaster affecte d areas, within a week of the disaster  for quick and 
initial assessment of the damage .  Further, if preliminary damage assessment is done jointly 
with the concerned State Governments then chances of differences in assessment of damage is 
likely to be minimized. 
 (Para 3.4.8)  
 
 The Committee appreciates the work done by NDRF for disaster management in the 
country. The Committee also takes note of the efforts made by the MHA in setting up disaster 
management teams. The Committee recommends possession of adeq uate manpower and 
infrastructure in the regional response centres for the swift movement of the troops in case of 
a disaster. 
 (Para 3.4.10) 
 
 The Committee understands that vagaries of nature cannot be controlled through 
policy but sound policy can be evo lved so that loss of lives, livestock and property can be 
minimized by taking timely steps to remain prepared for the disaster. However by taking 
adequate repair/compensation measures rehabilitation of the victims can also be done. The 
Committee notes that rehabilitation and infrastructure restoration, etc., has to be done by the 
concerned departments of the Central Government and the State Governments which creates 
compartmentalization of reaction to the disasters.  Therefore the Committee recommends 
that the MHA needs to strengthen its role to coordinate amongst all the agencies both in the 
States or in the Centre, who are involved in restoration and rehabilitation work, so that the 
relief measures are taken within a fixed time frame. 
 (Para 3.4.11) 
             
 
 The Committee takes note of the above measures and feels the need to prepare and  
engage communities to deal with all phases of a Disaster: preparedness, prevention, 
mitigation, response, and recovery . To build disaster resilient communities, the c ommunities 
need to be empowered first so that it can cope with the adverse effects of natural hazards. 
This is the most sustainable approach in dealing with disaster risks.  The Committee strongly 
recommends that in the pattern of National Cadet Corps (NCC) , a D isaster Management 
Training Corps (DMTC) can be initiated in schools and colleges not only to play the role of a 
strong civilian corps to support the Disaster Management Teams but also to disseminate the 
practices in disaster management at the community level.

 The Committee is surprised to note that the GNCTD has not able to address the issues 
of two landfill sites in th e national capital. The Committee firmly believes that there is an 
urgent need to find a permanent solution to the issue of landfills at Bhalswa and Ghazipur. 

 
 
122 
 
Therefore, the Committee recommends that a concrete plan should be chalked out in the 
matter. Fur ther, periodic consultation/review should be carried out between the MHA, 
GNCTD, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change and foreign experts groups 
and effective/regular monitoring to ensure the waste handling and management at these sites. 
 
 (Para 5.7.9)  
Demand No. 55 - Transfers to Jammu & Kashmir 
 
 The Committee notes that there exists a huge potential that can be explored in terms of 
exotic agrarian products, tourism and hospitality, industrial estates, handloom and 
handicrafts. But to reali se this potential, there is a need to improve the connectivity of J&K 
with the rest of India.  
 (Para 5.8.16) 
 
 To improve air connectivity, the Committee recommends that necessary measures must 
be taken to keep the airfares for J&K under a reasonable limi t. The Committee also 
recommends that the number of flights from Srinagar to Leh and from Srinagar to Kargil 
may be increased.  Given the mountainous terrain and the frequency of landslides in the 
region, the Committee recommends that helicopter services m ay be further augmented by 
putting additional helicopters into service for tourist facilitation. Lesser -known and far flung 
destinations like Gurez, Bangus, Kishtwar, etc. should remain connected throught these 
additional helicopter services. Tourist schem es should also be devised efficiently so as to 
connect Srinagar with other major cities, especially in the peak tourist season.  
 
 (Para 5.8.17) 
 
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs along with the J&K 
Government should engage with t he Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Airports Authority of 
India, to facilitate the operation of international flights from Sheikh ul -Alam Airport, 
Srinagar. The Committee also recommends that the infrastructure provided at Srinagar 
Airport must be improved for the same. 
 
 (Para 5.8.18) 
 
 To boost handicraft industry in J&K, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of 
Home Affairs should take up with the Ministry of Finance seeking some exemption to 
handloom and handicrafts under the implementation of GS T to ensure a market for the 
handloom and handcrafted products which are presently underperforming due to 
competition with cheap imports. The Committee recommends that the State Government may 
introduce skilled craft in the curriculum in order to educate c hildren about the rich 
traditional handloom and handicrafts heritage of the UT. This will also go a long way in 
ensuring livelihood in the UT, whilst ensuring the longevity of these prized handloom and 
handicraft skills. 
 (Para 5.8.19) 
 
 The Committee emphasizes the need for proper physical and social infrastructures like 
land, capital, storage, roads, railways, air connectivity, communication, power, skilled 

 
 
123 
 
workforce to attract new industries and entrepreneurs into J&K. The Committee also 
recommends setti ng up a Planning Board and investment promotion agency in J&K in a 
stipulated time to formulate investment plans and coordinate with the industries from various 
sectors and countries to increase investment in J&K. The MHA should also hold periodic 
meetings with the Planning Board for guidance and addressing the issues with the concerned 
Ministries of the Government of India. 
 
 (Para 5.8.20) 
Employment 
 
 The Committee notes that there are vacancies of 22078, 54375 and 7552 at Class IV, 
Non-Gazetted and Gazetted level, respectively and their recruitment will be done by the Staff 
Selection Board. The Committee recommends to expedite the recruitment process and fill the 
vacancies in a time bound manner. The Committee further recommends to reserve seats for 
the lo cal youth so that they can get due share in the Government jobs of the UT. The 
Committee also recommends the administration of the UT of J&K to assess the requirement 
of manpower after being established as a UT and notify it on a priority basis. 
 
 (Para 5.8.22) 
Demand No. 56 - Transfers to Puducherry 
 
 The Committee takes note of the optimal utilization of funds by the UT of Puducherry 
in FY 2019 -20. The Committee notes that against the projected demand of Rs. 2810.02 crore 
in 2020 -21 only Rs. 1703.02 crore  has been granted to the UT. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that MHA must pursue with the Ministry of Finance, citing the healthy trend of 
expenditure by the UT, for allocation of adequate funds under the projected demand of the 
Government of Puducherry. The Committee, further recommends the MHA to consider the 
restoration of 90:10 pattern for CSS in the UT of Puducherry as it is in the sensitive coastal 
region and has constituent districts in three States and therefore, needs more funds for 
development and administration of districts and preservation of eco-sensitive zone. 
 
(Para 5.9.4)

CHAPTER -I 
OVERVIEW 
1.1 Introduction 
1.1.1 India‟s North Eastern Region (NER) comprises of eight States - Arunachal Pradesh, 
Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Miz oram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. The NER is unique in 
terms of growth opportunities as the region possesses the potential to develop into an economic 
powerhouse, being a vibrant source of energy, oil, natural gas, coal, and limestone. Besides being 
endowed with India‟s largest perennial water system in the river Brahmaputra and its tributaries , 
the NER is also home to a great variety of horticultural products, plantation crops, vegetables, 
spices, rare herbs and medicinal plants. The region also offers v ast tourism opportunities, rare 
flora and fauna, breathtaking natural beauty, a rich culture of performing arts besides varied 
cuisine and handicrafts. 
1.1.2 To coordinate the developmental efforts being taken by the Central and the State 
Governments in th e NER, the Department of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) 
was set up in 2001. Subsequently, the Department was upgraded to a full -fledged Ministry in 
May 2004 . I t is the only Ministry with a territorial jurisdiction.   The Ministry of DoNER 
implements the schemes of Non -Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) that have been 
restructured as North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) and Special 
Packages through State Governments of NER and some Central Ministries . The North E astern 
Council (NEC), Shillong, which was set up in 1971, is under the administrative control of 
Ministry of DoNER.  There are two Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs), namely, North 
Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Ltd. (NEHH DC) and North 
Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Ltd. (NERAMAC), under M/o DoNER. 
 
1.2 Coordination with Central Ministries and Departments  
1.2.1 In October 1996, it was decided that Central Ministries/ Departments, unless specifically 
exempted, will set apart 10 per cent of their Plan Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) for the NER to 
ensure a quantum jump in budgetary resource flow to the region and to fill the backlog and gaps 
in basic minimum services and infrastructure.  Subsequently, funds  for the NER are being 
allocated annually on a lump sum basis by the non -exempted Central Ministries/Departments at 
the BE/RE stage, under the Major Heads 2552 (for revenue expenditure), 4552 (for capital 
expenditure) and 6552 (for loan expenditure). These  funds are expended under their respective 
functional schemes. These schemes may either be in the form of direct intervention by the 
Ministries/Departments or through their institutions/agencies or may even be through the 
concerned State Governments. 
1.2.2 The Ministry of DoNER, being the nodal Ministry, coordinates with the various 
Ministries/ Departments primarily concerned with development and welfare activities in the 
NER and keeps track of expenditure under the mandatory 10 per cent GBS by the non -exempted 
Ministries/ Departments since its inception. This exercise is being undertaken on an annual basis

1.5 Central Pool of Resources for NER 
1.5.1 In 1997-98, when it was found that the actual expenditure of Ministries/Departments for 
NER was less than the mandatory c eiling of 10 per cent, the Government took the decision to 
create a “Central Resource Pool” into which the unutilized portion of the 10 per cent earmarked 
GBS would accrue at the end of the financial year.  Since 1998 -99, the annual surrendered 
amounts out of the earmarked outlays of all the non -exempted Central Ministries/Departments 
for NER have been accounted as accruals to this Pool and the annual expenditure of the Ministry 
under the NLCPR scheme is being accounted as withdrawal from the Pool. However,  this is a 
notional pool, maintained on a proforma basis by the Ministry of Finance. The Ministry of 
DoNER monitors Ministry -wise expenditure/ surrendered amounts for the purpose of 
ascertaining the accrual to the NLCPR pool in consultation with the Ministry of Finance. 
1.6 Re-appropriation Mechanism 
1.6.1 The Ministry of DoNER has been conferred with the powers to review the quarterly 
expenditure of the non -exempted Ministries and recommend reallocation of likely surrendered 
amount to those Ministries/Depa rtments, which have the absorptive capacity to implement 
additional approved schemes/programmes within the financial year.  
 
INSTITUTIONS UNDER MINISTRY OF DONER 
1.7 North Eastern Council (NEC) 
1.7.1 The NEC was constituted as a statutory advisory body und er the NEC Act 1971 (84 of 
1971) marking the beginning of a new chapter of concerted and planned endeavor for rapid 
socio-economic development of the North Eastern Region (NER) and is under the administrative 
control of the Ministry of DoNER.  It is a statu tory Regional Planning Body, which provides 
financial assistance for a variety of projects including infrastructure projects like construction of 
roads, improving air connectivity, etc., through State Governments.  
1.8 Cane and Bamboo Technology Centre (CBTC) 
1.8.1 Cane and Bamboo Technology Centre (CBTC) is an ISO 9001:2008 certified 
organization and was established in the year 2000 as part of Cane and Bamboo Technological 
Upgradation and Networking Programme of United Nations Development Programme (UNDP),  
where the Department of Science & Technology (DST), Govt. of India and United Nations 
Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) were the main stakeholder s. CBTC has been 
registered as a Society on 21 st July, 2004 with Secretary NEC as Chairman. It works  for the 
development of the cane and bamboo sector in the country especially in the NE Region.  

5 
 
1.9 North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited 
(NEHHDC) 
1.9.1 NEHHDC was set up in 1977 at Shillong, Meghalaya, with the mandate of promotion and 
development of handicrafts and handlooms sectors in the NER of the country.  NEHHDC plays a 
key role in the development and promotion of the Handicrafts and Handlooms sectors of the 
North Eastern Region. NEHHDC has been providing Marketing s upport through procurement of 
Handicrafts and Handlooms products directly from the Artisans, Weavers, Self -Help Groups at 
clusters and selling the same through its Sales Emporia located at Shillong, Guwahati, Kolkata, 
New Delhi and Gujarat and through Sale s Promotion Offices located at Chennai and Bangalore 
and also through conduct of various exhibition and marketing events all over the country. 
1.10 North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC)  
1.10.1 North Eastern Regional Agricultu ral Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC) Limited was 
incorporated in the year 1982 as a Government of India Enterprise under the administrative 
control of the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER).  
1.10.2 NERAMAC has been envisaged and functioning as a marketing organization dedicated to 
the agricultural sector of the North-eastern region and is lending a supporting hand to the farmers 
right from the fields and up to the markets to the end consumers for their produces. NERAMAC 
procures produces from the farmers at remunerative prices and maintains the supply chain for 
proper distribution and placing of produces in the markets throughout the country.   
 
LIVELIHOOD, ENTREPRENEURSHIP, CAPACITY BUILDING, ADVOCACY & 
PUBLICITY 
1.11 North East Rural Livelihood project (NERLP) 
1.11.1 North East Rural Livelihood Project (NERLP), a World Bank aided project was launched 
in 2012. It was implemented by Ministry of Development o f North Eastern Region (MDoNER)  
to improve rural livelihoods especially that of wo men, unemployed youth and the most 
disadvantaged people by building community based organizations and developing partnership 
with Government and other institutions for knowledge, skill, credit, insurance, extension and 
market. 
1.12 North Eastern Region Community Resource Management Project (NERCORMP) 
1.12.1 NEC supports Community Based Sustainable Livelihood Projects i.e., North Eastern 
Region Community Resource Management Project (NERCORMP), which was launched in May, 
1999. 
1.13 North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Limited (NEDFi) 
1.13.1 The North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Limited (NEDFi) was incorporated 
as a public limited company under the Companies Act, 1956, in 1995. It is notified as a Public 
Financial Institution under Section 4A of the said Act and was registered as an NBFC [Non -

6 
 
Depository-Systemically Important (ND -SI)] in 2002 with RBI. The core business of the 
Corporation comprises of lending activities (fund based) and fee based activities. The lending 
activities are undert aken through the project finance schemes and microfinance schemes. The 
Corporation also provides fee based Advisory & Consultancy Services. NEDFi plays an 
important role in facilitating setting up of new industrial and service sector projects in the North 
Eastern States. 
1.14 Science & Technology Intervention North Eastern Region (STINER) 
1.14.1 The new initiative for Science & Technology Intervention in North Eastern Region 
(STINER) was envisaged by M/o DoNER in close collaboration with the Office of Princ ipal 
Scientific adviser (PSA) to Govt. of India with an aim to improve the livelihood of vulnerable 
groups in a sustainable manner especially that of women, unemployed youth and the poor 
farmers and artisans of the North Eastern Region of the country. The Ministry‟s initiative in the 
form of STINER Project was officially transferred to North Eastern Council, Shillong along with 
a budget Provision of Rs. 40 crore (Rupees Forty crore) in June, 2016 for sanctioning funds to 
implement the project by CSIR-NEIST, Jorhat.

CHAPTER III 
NORTH EAST COUNCIL (NEC) AND RELATED SCHEMES 
3.1.1 The North Eastern Council which was set up as a Regional Advisory Body under the 
North Eastern Council Act, 1971 (Act No. 84 of 1971) was transformed into a Regional Planning 
Body by the 2002 amendment.  The relevant provision of the amended NEC Act is quoted 
below: - 
Section 4 of the original Act: 
 
“(a) for sub-sections (1) and (2), the following sub-sections shall be substituted, namely:- 
1. The Council shall function as a regional planning body for the North eastern area. 
2. While formulating the regional plans for the North eastern area, the Council shall give 
priority to schemes and projects, which will benefit two or more States: 
Provided that in case of Sikkim, the Council shall formulate specific projects and schemes for 
that State including the review of implementation of such project and schemes”. 
 
3.1.2 The Committee was informed that the above provision of the amended NEC Act 
mandated the North Eastern Council (NEC) to function as a “regional planning body for the 
North eastern area” with the tasks of formulating “regional plans for the North eastern area” that 
benefit two or more States. Given the smallness of majority of the State s in the region, in terms 
of landmass and population, it is advantageous for such States that regional plans are formulated 
in a coordinated manner for cohesive and integrated economic development for the region as a 
whole.

3.2.9 The Committee sought to know that h ow far the schemes of North Ea st Council, since

economic development of the region . The Ministry informed that i n the last forty -eight years, 
NEC has been instrumental in setting up iconic Institutes in the Region such as North East Police 

18 
 
Academy, Shillong, North Eastern Regional Institute of Science & Technology, Itanagar, 
Regional Institute of Paramedical & Nursing Sciences, Aizawl, Regional Institute of Medical 
Sciences, Imphal, North Eastern Regional Institute of Water and Land Management in Tezpur, 
Regional Institute of Pharmaceutical Science & Technology (RIPSAT), Agartala and others. A 
total of 10,911 kms of roads have been constructed with the NEC funding and handed over to the 
States for maintenance. NEC has supported the installation of 694.5 MW of power plants and

& Horticulture, Fisheries and Art & Culture etc.  
  
3.2.10 The Committee was apprised that t he implementation of projects in the NE s tates faces 
unique challenges, especially short working season and lack of big infrastructure contracting 
firms. However, in recent years the situation and implementing capacities has considerably 
improved in project implementations by the States and Agencies.  
 
3.2.11 The Ministry informed that the main bottlenecks faced by the NEC were large amount of 
unspent balances; late receipt of Utilization Certificates (UCs); delay in awarding the work; 
delay in release of funds by State Governments to implementing  agencies; and issues related to 
land acquisition and forest clearances.  These have been addressed by frequent reviews, use of 
technology and by modifying guidelines of the schemes. It has further been decided that in 
future, no project will be sanctioned  unless the land is available free from all encumbrances; all 
forest and other regulatory clearances are available.  The use of space technology through North-
Eastern Space Applications Centre  (NESAC) by satellite mapping of proposed and ongoing 
projects a nd geo -tagging would be adopted intensively to overcome the geographical and 
physical challenges.   
3.2.12 The Committee appreciates the role of the NEC in formulation of regional plans for 
integrated and balanced socio-economic development of the NER.  Therefore, it is pertinent 
that NEC   must synchronise the efforts made under central projects/schemes and efforts of 
the State Government of NE regions to achieve the objectives of inclusive growth and 
equitable distribution of benefits of socio -economic development to the lower rungs of the 
society. The Committee also takes note of the efforts made by the NEC  to liquidate the 
huge committed liabilities against ongoing and completed projects which depend on receipt 
of utilization certificates from State Gove rnments and implementing agencies respectively.  
The Committee recommends  that the Ministry must put all  its efforts for clearing of 
liabilities of on-going projects and undertake strict measures to resolve the issues of non -
receipt of Utilization Certificates from the State Governments for the future projects. 
3.2.13 During the Committee's meeting held on 19th Februray 2020, the Committee sought to 
know whether there is proper method of having coordination amongst the three agencies that is 
M/o DoNER, NEC and the State Governments  and why there are these three levels . The 
Ministry replied that NEC was set up as a planning body for the NER.  As per revised 
guidelines issued in 2018, a sector -specific division of work has been made between NEC and 

19 
 
MDoNER. There is no overlapping jurisdiction between NEC and MDoNER.  Practically only 
two levels are working in NER like other parts of the country. All the S tate Sector Schemes are 
implemented through State Governments only, (except  Projects involving two or more States) 
and Central Sector Schemes through concerned line Departments only. 
3.2.14 The Committee notes the 2018 guidelines wherein sector specific divison of work has 
been made between NEC and MDoNER but it feels that there is a need to re-look, re-invent 
and re-define the roles of M/o DoNER, NEC and the State Governments.

3.6 North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) 
3.6.1 The Cabinet has approved a new scheme of North East Special Infrastructure 
Development Scheme (NESIDS) on 15.12.2017 restructuring the existing NLCPR scheme of 
Ministry of DoNER.  NESIDS has been approved for a period of three years i.e. from 2017-18 to 
2019-20 at a total cost of Rs.1600.00 crore. 
  
3.6.2 The broad objective of NESIDS is to ensure focused development of North East Region 
by providing financial assistance for the projects of:  
 
a. Physical infrastructure sectors relating to water supply, power, connectivity to enhance 
tourism;   
b.  Social sector of education and health for creation of infrastructure in the areas of 
primary and secondary sectors. 
3.6.3 The Projects taken up under NESIDS will be 100% funded by Government of India . 
While identifying the projects, emphasis will be given to the backward areas by earmarking 25% 
share for them.   The NESIDS will be over and above the existing schemes of Government of 
India and State Governments of the NE Region. Under the scheme, only t hose projects would be 
taken up which are not covered under any scheme of Government of India or the State 
Government. The NLCPR saving s of  Rs. 402.47 crore has been carried forward to NESIDS. 
Since approval of NESIDS on 15.12.2017, projects worth Rs.1904. 94 crore have already been 
selected for funding out of which 57 projects worth Rs. 1799.28 crore have been sanctioned so 
far.

approved estimated amount and release of funds.

5.2 North Eastern Handicrafts and Handlooms Development Corporation Limited 
(NEHHDC) 
5.2.1 The North Eastern Handicrafts and handlooms Development Corporation Ltd(NEHHDC) 
was established in M arch 1977 with the mandate of promotion and development of handicrafts 
and handlooms of the North Eastern Region and to provide the needed marketing support to the 
artisans and weavers of the Region. 
 
5.2.2 The Ministry informed that in order to achieve th ese broad objectives, the Corporation 
has been facing several challenges. The challenges faced by the Corporation are as under- 
 
(i) Lack of infrastructure/ Showroom/ Warehouse : NEHHDC has 11 small and bigger 
showrooms/ Emporium in the country located  in Shill ong, Ambari, Guwahati , 

41 
 
Kolkata, New Delhi, Bangalore, Chennai and Emporium at Kevadia, Gujarat. But in 
order to penetrate the market, NEHHDC requires a wider retail sales base in the form 
of showrooms in high footfall areas with warehouse facilities 
(ii) Inadequate profit margin out of promotional events : At times the administrative 
expenses incurred in organizing/ participating in such promotional events exceeds the 
profit earned out of such events; 
(iii)Inadequate Publicity and Branding :   In order to make the wide  range of North East 
handicrafts and handlooms products popular, adequate publicity and branding is 
required. NEHHDC has not been able to undertake these activities on a larger way 
which results in sluggish turnover. 
(iv) High Cost of sourcing and procurement:   The artisans and weavers are located in far 
flung interior land locked areas leading to higher cost of souring and procurement. 
This results in high Selling price leading to stiff competition in the market. 
(v) Transportation bottlenecks : As Northeast is main ly in the hilly terrain the 
transportation costs of products sourced and procured from the artisans/weavers is 
high, leading to comparatively high Selling price of the products.  
(vi) Constraints of quality Raw material : The main raw materials for the handicraf ts and 
handlooms sectors in the region are bamboo, cane, sitalpati, jute, kauna, water 
hyacinth, cotton and silk yarns and other natural fibbers. The cane reserves are fast 
dwindling and are expensive.  Cotton   yarns in the region come from the mills from  
Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu. Dyes and chemicals manufacturers are also 
not available in the North Eastern Region. This has resulted in making the handlooms 
and handicraft products expensive and NEHHDC faces challenges for marketing 
North East handlooms and handicrafts products. 
(vii) Lack of Mass production:  NEHHDC receives bulk orders for certain products. The 
artisans and weavers produce a large variety of products but there has always been a 
constraint in mass production which hampers bulk supply orders. 
(viii) Lack of design Intervention/ Standardization/Packaging : NEHHDC organises 
design workshops and projects for product development, Awareness for 
standardization of products and packaging at cluster level for handlooms and 
handicrafts products. Due to fund constraints NEHHDC is unable to provide adequate 
Training and conduct Awareness Programme.  
 
5.2.3 The Ministry also stated the efforts undertaken by the Ministry to overcome the above 
challenges which are as follows:  
 
(i) The Ministry has been providing working capital loan of   Rs.2.00 crore per annum to the 
corporation to meet its working capital requirement for sourcing and procurement of 
handloom and handicraft products from the artisans and weavers of the region and to 
provide them the needed marketing platform.  
(ii) The Ministry has also been supporting by providing funds for implementation of 
workshops, seminars and   Training programmes for the benefits of the artisans and 
weavers of the region. 
(iii)The ministry has been supporting NEHHDC in publicity and ma rketing of the handloom 
and handicraft products by   conducting Exhibitions/Expos/ fairs etc in the country. 

42 
 
(iv) The Ministry has been supporting in maximising the reach of the NEHHDC by providing 
funds to participate in overseas exhibitions and business meets. 
(v) In order to boost the market of indigenous products the Ministry provides funds for 
registration of handlooms and handicrafts products under Geographical Indication 
(GI).

6.1 Vision 2020 
 
6.1.1 The Committee was apprised about the details of the Vision 2020 Document which 
provides an overarching framework for the development of the North Eastern Region to bring  it 
at par with other developed regions under which different Ministries, including Ministry of 
Development of North Eastern Region have undertaken various initiatives. 
 
6.1.2 The Ministry informed that strengthening infrastructure and connectivity is a ma jor thrust 
area identified by the Vision document. Several connectivity initiatives have been undertaken, 
which inter alia, include the Special Accelerated Road Development Programme for North East 
(SARDP-NE), in which a total of 3029 Km (2101 km SARD -NE P hase - A and 928 Km 
Arunachal Pradesh Packages) have been constructed up to 2018 -19 with expenditure of Rs. 
30315 crore under SARDP -NE Scheme. New Capital connectivity by rail to Gangtok, Aizwal, 
Kohima and Imphal is likely to be established by 2022. All t he Meter Gauge sections in the 
entire North East region were converted in to Broad Gauge by 2017. In the last three years 
(2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20), new lines of 167.75 km have been completed and 89.84 km of 
doubling has been done.  Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh have been connected by 
Rail Network in the last five years . Agartala -Akhaura Rail -Link will connect the existing 
Agartala station in Tripura to Akhaura station of Bangladesh Railways by 2021. There are 13 
operational airports in the region providing connectivity to the North Eastern States with the help 
of more than 1700 flights per week. A Greenfield Airport (Pakyong) near Gangtok has been 
constructed. The Greenfield airport at Hollongi near Itanagar with a project cost of Rs. 955.67  
crore has been sanctioned for completion in 2022. Development of River Barak waterway, for 
shipping and navigation purposes, is under implementation and 18 other rivers have been 
undertaken. Comprehensive Telecom Development Project (CTDP) with a cost of Rs. 8120.81 
crore for mobile connectivity and Bharat Net in NER with an estimated project cost of Rs. 2500 
crore for providing broadband connectivity to all GPs is under implementation.   
 
6.1.3 The Committee was informed that a  number of sectoral initiati ves, some with specific 
dispensations, have been undertaken to promote livelihoods keeping in view the areas in which 
the region has comparative advantage. Realizing the potential of organic farming in the North 
Eastern Region, the Mission Organic Value Ch ain Development for North Eastern Region 
scheme aims at development of certified organic production in a value chain mode to build up a 
bridge between growers and consumers and to support the sustainable development of entire 
value chain starting from inpu ts, seeds, planting materials, certification, to the creation of 
facilities for collection, post -harvest management, aggregation, processing marketing and brand 
building initiative. The main focus of the scheme is on export of produces. The scheme was 
approved with an outlay of Rs.400 crore for three years. 
 
6.1.4 The Ministry further informed the Committee that it had been implementing two 
Livelihood Schemes, namely, North East Rural Livelihood Project (NERLP) and North Eastern 
Region Community Resource Ma nagement Project (NERCORMP) in the North Eastern States.

6.7 Waterways 
 
6.7.1 The Ministry stated that the Government of India through various policies  has taken a big 
leap in developing Inland Waterways (IWs) in North Eastern Region. There are 20 National 
Waterways (NWs) in North Eastern Region (NER) including River Brahmaputra (NW -2) and 
River Barak (NW -16).  River Brahmaputra was declared as NW in the  year 1988, while River 
Barak and other 18 rivers of NER were declared as NWs in April 2016 vide National Waterways 
Act, 2016. 
6.7.2 During the Committee's meeting held on 19th Februray 2020, the Committee sought to 
know the s tatus of Water ways in Brahmap utra  river from Kolkata/Chittagong ports. The 
Ministry replied that  Inland Water Transit and Trade Protocol exists between India and 
Bangladesh under which the two Governments agreed to make mutually beneficial arrangement 
for the use of their waterways f or trade and for transit cargo from Indian mainland (Kolkata) to 
NE region. Under the Indo -Bangladesh inland water transit and trade protocol routes valid for 7 
years, the   development of fairway in Ashuganj -Zakiganj of River Kushiyara in Bangladesh for 
connecting NW16 (River Barak)and Sirajganj-Daikhowa of River Jamuna in Bangladesh stretch, 
the dredging and allied work is under progress and both the routes from Kolkata/Haldia Ports to 
NER via Brahmaputra and via Barak through Bangladesh would be operational by 2020.  
6.7.3 The Ministry further stated that the Ministry of Shipping, Govt. of India has signed an 
agreement with Govt. of Bangladesh regarding use of Chattogram (Chittagong) and Mongla 
Ports in Bangladesh for movement of goods to and from India w hich will bring revolutionary 
cost-cutting in  shipments to and from the North Eastern States. In this regard, a Standard 
Operating Procedure (SOP) wherein Bangladesh allowed the use of its Chattogram and Mongla 
Ports for movement of goods to and from India  through its territory was signed on 05.10.2019. 
The agreement and SOP permit the movement of goods in Bangladesh through waterways, rail, 
road or multi-modal transport. Eight (08) routes are provided under the Agreement which would 
enable access of North East Region (NER) via Bangladesh. The routes are: 
(i) Chattogram/Mongla Port to Agartala (Tripura) via Akhura 
(ii) Chattogram/Mongla Port to Dawki (Meghalaya) via Tamabil 
(iii)Chattogram/Mongla Port to Sutarkandi (Assam) via Sheola 
(iv) Chattogram/Mongla Port to Srimantpur (Tripura) via Bibirbazar (and vice versa)  
6.7.4 The Committee was informed that the conclusion of the SOP on Chattogram and  Mongla 
ports  would reduce distance, time and logistic cost for transport of goods. Three landlocked 
states of India viz. Assam, Me ghalaya and Tripura will get access to open sea trade routes from 
Chattogram and Mongla ports via Indian ports. Cargo transportation through IBP waterway route 
from Kolkata/Haldia to North East is limited to 2000 ton vessels. Now, larger ships carrying 
cargo destined for North East can call at Chattogram and Mongla ports thereby increasing trade 
volumes and reducing logistic costs.

6.9 Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport (KMTT) Project 
 
6.9.1 The Committee was informed that in accordance with the Act East Policy of the 
Government, the Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport (KMTT) Project was conceptualized by 
the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) to provide an alternative connectivity to Mizoram with 
Haldia/Kolkata ports through the Kaladan River in Myanmar. Kaladan Multi Mo dal Transit 
Transport Project (KMMTTP) will create a multi -modal transport corridor for shipment of cargo 
from the eastern ports of India to Myanmar as well as North -Eastern part of India via Myanmar. 
The project includes a waterway component of 158 km on Kaladan river from Sittwe to Paletwa 
in Myanmar and a road component of 109 km from Paletwa to Zorinpui on the India -Myanmar 
border in Mizoram State. A Framework Agreement between GOI and Myanmar in this was 
signed in 2008. 
6.9.2 The Ministry informed that  Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) is the Project 
Development Consultant for the waterways component of the project and M/s. Ircon 
Infrastructure Services Ltd. is Project Management Consultant for the road component. Work of 
construction of waterw ays component was awarded to M/s. Essar Project (India) Limited in 
2010. The Estimated cost of the project is Rs. 2904.04 crore (Rs 982.99 crore for waterways and 
Rs 1921.05 crore for road component) as approved by the Cabinet in October 2015. Work for 
construction of road has been awarded to M/s. EPI -C&C JV in March 2017. Expenditure 
incurred so far on Kaladan project is Rs. 639.93 crore (Rs. 519.88 crore towards waterways 
component and Rs. 120.05 crore towards road component).The originally approved works  under 
waterways have been completed in May 2017 and a port operator has been appointed for 
operation and maintenance of the waterways component on 1 February 2020.Work for 
construction of road was to take 3 years to complete. 
6.9.3 The Ministry further informed that the physical progress of road construction work is not 
at all satisfactory. Acute financial crisis faced by JV partner M/s. C&C, delayed action by JV 
partner M/s. EPIL, non -availability of access to the project site from India -Myanmar border in  
Mizoram and adverse security situation in the project area are the main reasons for delays in the 
project. 
6.9.4 The Committee takes note of the progress of the Kaladan Multimodal Transit 
Transport (KMTT) project that is being piloted and funded by the Mi nistry of External 
Affairs. The Committee is displeased to note that the physical progress of road construction 
work is not at all satisfactory. The Committee understands that this project is an integral 
part of the Act East Policy of India and  will contribute to the economic development in the 

56 
 
whole Region. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the reasons for delay must be 
addressed soon and the project should be closely monitored. The Committee further 
recommends that the progress should be reviewed regularly to complete the project at the 
earliest so that the connectivity woes of the North Eastern Region are resolved.

bilateral, regional and multilateral levels which would eventually provide enhanced connectivity

(i)  Agartala-Akhaura new rail link project 
6.12.3 Agartala-Akhaura new rail link project is a 12.24 km (5.50 km in India and       6.80 km in 
Bangladesh) cross-border rail connectivity of Agartala (Tripura) -Akhaura (Bangladesh). This is a 
dual gauge pr oject (BG/MG). This will enable alternate and shorter (by 1000 km) transit route 
from Kolkata to Agartala. The sanctioned cost of the project is Rs. 972 crore (Indian portion - Rs 
580 crore & Bangladesh portion - Rs 392 crore).  Financial progress in Indian side is 25%  and 
that for Bangladesh side is 29%  as on 31.12.2019.  Physical progress is 29% on Indian side and 
25% on Bangladesh side. The project is likely to be completed by 2021. 
(ii) Kaladan Multi Modal Transit Transport Project (KMMTTP) in Myanmar 
6.12.4 The Project includes two components , a waterway connection from S ittwe Port and a 
road hereafter to Indo-Mayanmar Border in Mizoram.    
6.12.5 The  Waterway segment of 158 km including  Port at Sittwe and inland waterway on  
Kaladan river from Sittwe to Paletwa in Myanmar was completed in May, 2017. A port operator 
has been appointed for operation and maintenance of the waterway component on 1st February 
2020. The Port has been handed over to Government of Myanmar. 
6.12.6 Work for construction of Road  (109 KM) was awarded to JV of EPIL and C&C 
Construction Limited. Work for construction of road was to take 3 years to complete (by May 
2020). The current physical progress for construction of road is behind the schedule. Acute 
financial crisis faced by JV  partner M/s. C&C, delayed action by JV partner M/s. EPIL, non -
availability of access to the project site from India -Myanmar border in Mizoram and adverse 
security situation in the project area are the main reasons for delays in the project. The physical 
progress is only 3 percent. Only recently necessary clearance for movement of men and material 
through Mizoram has been obtained and work has resumed. It is likely to take  another three 
years (2023-24) for completion of the Project.  
(iii) India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway 
6.12.7 India has undertaken two projects in Myanmar under the Trilateral Highway that starts 
from Moreh in India to Mae Sot in Thailand through Myanmar (Total length of 1360 kms): 
(i) Upgradation/construction of 69 bridges includi ng approach roads on the Tamu -Kyigone 
Kalewa (TKK) section of 150 kms.  
6.12.8 Implementation of the project was awarded to Joint Venture of M/s Niraj Cement 
Structural Ltd and M/s Manipur Tribal Development Corporation Ltd. (M/s NCSL -MTDCL JV) 
at the cost of Rs 293.94 crore in October 2017. The project commenced in November 2017 after 
signing of contract agreement and handing over of Right of Way to contractor.

          (ii)  Construction of 120 km of Kalewa-Yagyi section to highway standard.

6.16.1 The Committee sought to know the conservation measures taken for protection of  Majuli 
island. The Ministry informed that The Brahmaputra Board took up measures for protection of 
Majuli Island from floods and erosion in January 2 004, under „Immediate Measures‟ at a cost of 
Rs. 6.09 crore and completed in February 2005. These works were followed by protection works 
under Phase –I (revised cost Rs. 56.07 crore). All works under Phase -I were completed in April 
2011 at the expenditure of Rs. 52.63 crore. Brahmaputra Board also executed „Emergent Works‟ 
at the estimated cost of Rs. 4.75 crore for protection of Majuli island, on the recommendations of 
Standing Committee of Experts, in the year 2008. Phase -II & III works, at an estimated cost of 
Rs. 115.99 crore, are completed in November, 2019 and expenditure incurred up to November, 
2019 is Rs.127.59 crore. 
 
6.16.2 The Ministry further informed that a comprehensive proposal “Protection of Majuli Island 
from flood and erosion of river Brah maputra” has now been framed to take up anti erosion 
measures in all major erosion reaches of the southern bank of Island to provide reasonable 
protection against Flood & Erosion. The estimated cost of the Project is Rs. 233.57 crore 
(Rupees Two hundred th irty three crores and fifty seven lakhs only). Out of the total estimated 
provision of Rs. 233.57 crore, an amount of Rs 207.00 crore was agreed to be funded by 
Ministry of DONER from NLCPR - Central. With the implementation of the project, it is 
proposed to effectively protect vulnerable reaches of 80.00 km bank line on the right bank of 
river Brahmaputra along Majuli Island.  
 
6.16.3 The Ministry further informed that Rs.207 crore has been released to Brahmaputra Board 
under this project. Physical progress  of the scheme upto December, 2019 is 70.61% with an 
expenditure of Rs 131.88 crore. The project is planned to be completed by March, 2020.

Island from flood and erosion of river Brahmaputra‖ upto December, 2019 is 70.61% while

(Para  6.1.8)

Status of Infrastructural Projects under NLCPR , NESIDS, NERSDS and NEC Schemes 
 
The Committee notes that there are Institutions of higher learning of good standard in 
every State of North East but recommends that  steps should be taken for skill development 
and specialised vocational training of the youth in every State. 
(Para 6.3.6) 
 
Status of Major Roads 
 
The Committee observes that Projects under Tranche -I became effective from October, 
2012 and Projects under Tranche -II became effective from May, 2014. The Committee is 
not satisfied with the progress achieved in half a decade and feels that the construction on 
these stretches should have been completed by now. The Committee , recommends that the 
Ministry must urgently conduct an audit of construction activities of these roads and must 
seek explanation from the PWDs for the extremely snail -pace of the works pertaining to 
these roads. The Committee further recommends that the M inistry of DoNER should form 
an inspection team of officers from the Ministries of DoNER and Road Transport and 
Highways to visit the project sites, take photographs there and put them on internet and 
also review the construction activities of roads.  
(Para 6.5.9) 
 
Civil Aviation 
The Committee hopes that with the completion of ongoing/new projects would smoothen 
the air connectivity and operational efficacy of Civil Aviation in NER. The Committee 
recommends that these ongoing projects be completed in the st ipulated time frame and 
without cost overruns. The Committee desires that the Ministry of DoNER should 
coordinate with the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the State Governments concerned and 
remove the bottlenecks, if any, in implementation of the projects undertaken.  
(Para 6.6.7) 
 
 
Flood Control Projects 
 
 The Committee notes that  191 projects were sanctioned under NEC/NLCPR 
(Central) Scheme in Anti -Erosion/Flood Control and Irrigation Sector out of which 63 
projects pertains to Anti -Erosion and Flood Cont rol and of which 27 projects have been 
completed. The Committee further notes that there are 36 on-going flood control projects 
under Schemes of North Eastern Council and NLCPR (Central).  The Committee is aware 
that every year flood causes havoc and timel y implementation of all flood control projects 
is critical to the development of North Eastern Region. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should ensure timely completion of all pending flood control 
projects in the North Eastern Region.  
(Para 6.8.2) 
 

72 
 
Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport (KMTT) Project 
 
The Committee takes note of the progress of the Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport 
(KMTT) project that is being piloted and funded by the Ministry of External Affairs. The 
Committee is displeased to note that the physical progress of road construction work is not 
at all satisfactory. The Committee understands that this project is an integral part of the 
Act East Policy of India and  will contribute to the economic development in the whole  
Region. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the reasons for delay must be 
addressed soon and the project should be closely monitored. The Committee further 
recommends that the progress should be reviewed regularly to complete the project at the 
earliest so that the connectivity woes of the North Eastern Region are resolved.  
(Para 6.9.4) 
 
Tourism 
 
 The Committee takes note of the projects related to tourism promotion that are 
being implemented under the NESIDS Scheme and hopes that with concerted eff orts to 
implement these projects, niche and high end tourism will be developed in the NER.  The 
Committee is however, not happy to note that the educational tourism has not been 
explored in an organized manner by NE States. The Committee therefore recommends that 
Ministry must take steps to explore educational tourism with an aim to make education 
more accessible and providing qualified Human Resource for Tourism and Allied services 
for North Eastern Region States. This will help in making North East India a preferred 
destination for visitors and tourists and generate a pool of qualified youth for handling 
tourism activities there. 
(Para 6.10.7) 
 
North East Industrial Development Scheme(NEIDS) 
 
 
The Committee is displeased to note that no fund has been sanct ioned under NEIDS and 
respective State Level Committees of NEIDS have not recommended release of funds to 
any company. The Committee therefore recommends that a strategy should be chalked out 
to implement the programme/action plan to boost integrated and b alanced 
industrialization in NER and to promote employment in the North East States. 
(Para 6.11.4) 
 
 
Act East Policy 
 
The Committee notes the status of major proposals under Act East Policy. The Committee 
notes the physical progress of 29% on Indian side a nd 25% on Bangladesh side of 
Agartala-Akhaura new rail link project and recommends that the project should be 
completed without any time and cost overruns.  The Committee is also not satisfied with 
the physical progress of road construction work of Kaladan Multi Modal Transit 
Transport Project and projects undertaken in India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral 

73 
 
Highway as t his indicates a failure of proper planning, monitoring and supervision. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the reasons for delay must be addressed soon and 
the projects should be closely monitored.  
(Para 6.12.11) 
 
Food Processing Sector 
The Committee takes note of the scheme called Mission Organic Value Chain Development 
(MOVCD) for North Eastern Region implemented by the Ministry of Agric ulture and 
Farmers' Welfare for providing cluster development. The Committee hopes that the 
undertaken scheme would promote integrated agriculture and food processing units in 
NER. The Committee also observes that the budgetary allocations under this schem e have 
not been optimally utilized and only 47.60% funds have been utilized in the year 2019 -20. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the fund utilisation should be improved under 
this scheme. The Committee, further recommends that the Ministry should  review the 
implementation status of MOVCD in NER and undertake appropriate measure to achieve 
the set targets.  
(Para 6.14.4) 
 
The Committee notes the progress being made in the Food Processing Sector and also the 
number of projects being taken up under t his sector. The Committee recommends that 
Ministry of DoNER must co -ordinate with implementing agencies and the line Ministries 
concerned for ensuring the speedy execution of undertaken projects at the specified pace.   
(Para 6.14.5) 
 
Environment and Forests 
 
The Committee feels that mere allocation and release of funds would not be effective in 
expanding the forest cover without robust and effective monitoring, and regular evaluation 
of the Green India Mission. The Committee, therefore, recommends that mea sures should 
be taken in various North Eastern states to intensify afforestation programmes. The 
Committee also desires to be apprised about the various outcomes achieved in different 
States of the NER as a result of implementation of Green India Mission.    
(Para 6.15.4) 
 
 
The Committee observes that there is a wide disparity in the North -Eastern Region as per 
the Sustainable Development Goals Index of NITI Aayog. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry must intensify their efforts and pursu e for additional 
allocations to reduce this wide regional disparity in the North-Eastern Region. 
(Para 6.15.6) 
 
 

74 
 
Majuli Island 
 
 
The Committee notes that Physical progress of the scheme ―Protection of Majuli Island 
from flood and erosion of river Brahmaput ra‖ upto December, 2019 is 70.61% while 
project is planned to be completed by March, 2020. This island requires great amount of 
attention to preserve the rich ancient culture, protect livelihoods and prevent erosion 
caused due to anthropogenic activities.  This calls for huge attention by administrators and 
efforts in collaboration and cooperation with several experts groups, agencies at local and 
global levels to promote the idea through reduced disaster risks.  The Committee therefore 
feels that the Minist ry needs to intensify its efforts to p rotect and preserve the island 
through institutional and community participation.  
(Para 6.16.4)

CHAPTER-I 
 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Government 
 
 
1.1 Allocation, projections and variations 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.1.1 The Committee also notes that there has been allocation of Rs. 105244.34 crore for the Police 
(Demand No.48) at BE 2020-21 that is around 7% more than last year’s allocation of Rs. 98202.23 
crore in BE 2019-20. The allocation made under the Revenue Head for the Police (Demand No.48) is 
Rs. 95397.97 crore at BE in 2020-21. The allocation made under  the Capital Head for the Police 
(Demand No.48) is Rs. 9846.37 crore at BE  in 2020-21 which is around 9% less than the allocation of 
Rs. 10790.28 crore under the capital head for the Police in BE 2019-20. This may hamper the creation 
of assets and negatively impact their capabilities. The Committee further observes reduction in 
allocation for the Border Infrastructure, Police Infrastructure, and Modernization of Police Forces in  
BE 2020 -21 over BE 2019-20. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should 
reconsider the requirements of the funds for the Police and Union Territories and pursue with the 
Ministry of Finance for increased allocation at the Revised Estimates stage. 
 
(Para 2.2.6 of 224th Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The requirement of funds would be re-assessed at RE 2020-21 stage and Ministry of Finance 
would be approached for increased allocation of funds, as recommended by the Committee. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
1.1.3 The Committee notes the reply. 
 
 
1.2 Allocation for the Union Territories 
  
Recommendation 
 
1.2.1 The Committee notes that the total allocation for the Union Territories in BE 2020-21 is Rs. 
52863.91 that is divided in to two parts. i.e. Union Territories (without legislature) is Rs. 19287.89 
crore and Union Territories (with legislature) is Rs. 33576.02 crore. The Committee notices that the 
total allocation for the Union Territories has been increased substantially mainly due to the allocation 
for the two newly created Union Territories of J&K and Ladakh. Further, for the Union Territories 
(without legislature), the allocation under the Revenue Head is Rs. 13787.02 i.e. 71.48% of total 
allocation to the UTs and Capital Head is Rs. 5536.57 i.e. 28.51% of the total allocation to the UTs. 
The Committee believes that the allocation under the Capital Head for the Union Territories (without 
legislature) should be increased for creation of assets particularly infrastructure, at a rapid rate and at 
the same time ensuring that the developmental projects of the UTs does not gets hampered due to 
shortage of funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must review the capital 
requirements of these UTs in the first half of the next fiscal year, expedite the developmental projects in 
the UTs and project a higher demand for allocation to the Ministry of Finance at RE stage. 
(Para 2.2.7 ibid) 

 
 
3 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.2.2 Recommendation of the Committee has been noted for compliance. All UT Administrations 
have been requested, vide this Ministry’s letter dated 06.05.2020, to expedite the developmental 
projects in the UTs and requirement of more/higher demand under Capital Head for allocation, if any, 
may be projected at RE/Supplementary stage, so that demands of UTs may be taken up with Ministry 
of Finance. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
1.2.3 The Committee notes the reply. 
 
 
1.3 Allocation Under Demand-46 (MHA) 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.3.1 The Committee notes that up to 30th January, 2020 the Ministry was able to spend  only 59.79 
percent of the total allocation granted under the combined Capital Head of Demand Nos. 46 and 48 in 
RE 2019-20. This was despite a reduction in allocation from Rs. 11129.62 crore in BE 2019-20 to Rs. 
10096.27 crore at RE stage under the combined Capital Head of Demand Nos. 46 and 48. The 
Committee fails to understand the reasons for this poor capital expenditure and wonders as to how the 
Ministry would be able to spend around the remaining 40 percent of the allocation under the Capital 
Head in limited days remaining in the current financial year. The Committee feels that a large sum of 
capital funds may have to be surrendered by the Ministry and it may subject them to further cuts. The 
Committee expresses its displeasure at this sub-optimal capital expenditure by the Ministry. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should try to remove all operational bottlenecks and 
undertake corrective measures to address the issues underlying the poor capital expenditure specially 
under demand No. 48 (Police). 
(Para 2.2.9 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.3.2 It is submitted that major allocations under the combined Capital Head of Demand Nos. 46 and 
48 were for Police Infrastructure, Border Infrastructure and Infrastructure for Disaster Management. 
 
1.3.3 Construction activities were speeded up after the monsoon season. Although the expenditure 
upto 30th January 2020 was only 59.79 percent of the total  budgetary allocation, at RE 2019-20 stage 
under the combined Capital Head of Demand Nos. 46 and 48, the final expenditure has been to the tune 
of 96.45 percent. 
 
1.3.4 It may also be pertinent to mention that in October 2019, the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India 
had halted all the construction activities in NCR of Delhi in the wake of very bad situation of pollution. 
This hampered various projects being undertaken by the Delhi Police and the construction of Central 
Armed Police Forces Institute of Medical Sciences (CAPFsIMS). 
 
1.3.5 Notwithstanding above, the Ministry is concerned with non-utilization of full budgetary 
provision under Capital Head of the Grants, especially under Demand No. 48- Police, and will take all 
corrective measures. 
 
 

 
 
4 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
1.3.6 The Committee notes that the Ministry has spent around 96.45% percent of the total 
allocation granted under the combined Capital Head of Demand Nos. 46 and 48 in RE 2019-20 at 
the end of the financial year 2019-20. The Committee, however, desires to be apprised about the 
completion status of the various projects being undertaken by the Delhi Police and the 
construction of Central Armed Police Forces Institute of Medical Sciences (CAPFsIMS).

1.6 National Disaster Response Fund 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.6.1 The Committee appreciates the work done by NDRF for disaster management in the country. 
The Committee also takes note of the efforts made by the MHA in setting up disaster management 
teams. The Committee recommends possession of adequate manpower and infrastructure in the 
regional response centres for the swift movement of the troops in case of a disaster. 
(Para 3.4.10 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
Possession of Adequate Manpower 
 
1.6.2 Based on the vulnerability profile of the country and to minimize the response time, NDRF 
teams are permanently available at 12 Battalion Headquarters and 27 Regional Response Centres 
(RRCs). In addition to above, keeping in view the operational requirements, teams are also kept at 11 
Tactically Pre-deployment Locations (TPLs) throughout the year. As such, NDRF teams are kept 
alert at 50 locations throughout the year to respond to emergent situations. Also, as per the 
requirements of the States/UTs during disasters or disasters like situations, additional teams are 
placed in sufficient numbers to provide prompt response. 
 
1.6.3 Further, Government of India has approved raising of 04 additional battalions of NDRF (02 
Bn from ITBP & 01 each from Assam Rifles and BSF), out of which 01 Battalion of Assam Rifle is 
inducted and undergoing Disaster Management Training. Remaining 03 Battalions are likely to be 
inducted by 2021. Induction of these additional 04 battalions will enhance the presence and activities 
of NDRF in coming years. 
 
 
 

 
 
6 
 
Infrastructure in the Regional Response Centres (RRC) 
 
1.6.4 A total 28 RRCs have been approved by MHA. 
 
(i) Infrastructure created at 4 RRC locations: Siliguri, Kolkata, Dwarka and Dehradun. 
(ii) Construction of infrastructure  is  under  progress  at  5  RRC  locations: Bengaluru, 
Balasore, Kishangarh, Supaul  & Vishakhapatnam and likely be completed by March 
2021. 
(iii) Land has been acquired for RRC at Gandhinagar; construction work will start in current 
financial year. 
(iv) Land has been acquired for 8 RRCs locations at: Agartala, Ernakulum, Gangtok, 
Lucknow, Port Blair, Nurpur, Hyderabad & Gorakhpur. EFC proposal of infrastructure 
for these 8 RRCs is under examination. 
(v) Land acquisition process for 3 RRCs locations at: Chennai, Ranchi and Dimapur is 
under progress in the concerned States, which may be finalized in current financial year. 
(vi) At other 7 RRCs locations: Aizwal, Mumbai, Noida, Bhopal, Srinagar, Panchkula & R K 
Puram (New Delhi) accommodation is being provided by the concerned States. 
 
1.6.5 Thus, all 28 RRCs are functioning from their respective approved locations at its own 
infrastructure or suitable accommodation provided by the States. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
1.6.6 The Committee notes the reply. However, the Committee further recommends that 
infrastructure and manpower requirements of the NDRF may be reviewed periodically.

1.8 Central Armed Police Forces 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.8.1 The Committee notes that the problem of poor mobile connectivity persists in areas of 
deployment of CAPFs personnel especially of Border Guarding Forces at Border out Posts. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should make efforts to strengthen mobile and internet 
connectivity, if not by the State-owned service providers, then by providing for the presence of private 
mobile service providers in such difficult areas so that regular mobile and internet services can be 
availed by every jawan on their own mobile phone devices. The proposal for providing Optical Fiber 
Cable (OFC) connectivity to all Border Out Posts (BOPs) by connecting all villages through National 
Optical Fiber Network must be considered on priority. Further, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry should periodically coordinate with the Ministry of Defence, DoT, Bharat Broadband 
Network Ltd. (BBNL) and other concerned agencies to address technical glitches, bottlenecks and 
delay in providing communication facilities to the CAPFs personnel particularly for them who are 
posted at borders. The Committee also desires to be apprised about the progress made in the ongoing 
proposal of diverting V-SAT terminals from Bharat Net Satellite GP Coverage Scheme and voice call 
facility using voice calling over the Internet/WiFi. 
(Para 4.3.16 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.8.2 Digital Satellite Phone Terminals (DSPTs) were sanctioned by MHA to CAPFs to enable their 
personnel to communicate with their family members from far flung/inaccessible areas of the country. 
These DSPT sites are provided subsidy from Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF), Department 
of Telecommunication (DoT). However, DSPT services completely stopped functioning w. e. f. 
13.05.2019 due to satellite shutdown. As a stop-gap arrangement, I-Sat phones were provided to 
CAPFs, but the number of I-Sat phones are less than the number of DSPTs. 
 
1.8.3 To find out a permanent solution for the problem, a meeting was convened in DoT on 21st 
January, 2020 which was attended by officials of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Border Roads 
Organization, Ministry of Defence, Army HQ, DCPW and Bharat Broadband Network Limited 
(BBNL). During the meeting following decisions were taken: 
 
(i) As a permanent solution to re-activate the connectivity to these locations, BBNL has been 
authorized to take up the work by diverting V-SAT terminals from the ongoing Bharat Net 
Satellite GP coverage scheme; 
(ii) Providing voice call facility using voice calling over Internet/ WiFi. MHA has examined the 
security implications for using voice over internet calls with the help of smart phone and 
provided its inputs to the DoT. 
(iii) As requested by DoT, the MHA has provided the list of reconfirmed DSPTs in respect of all 
CAPFs. 
 
1.8.4 DoT has informed that as per the approval of Digital Communications Commission, the work 
for re-provisioning of DSPTs has been awarded to BBNL and the project is being implemented by 
Telecommunications Consultants India Ltd. (TCIL). USOF, DoT is closely monitoring the re-
provisioning of DSPTs on regular basis. Due to ongoing COVID-19 situation, the implementing 
agency is facing lot of difficulties in transportation of material and movement of installation team. 
However, BBNL & TCIL in close co-ordination with MHA/MoD agencies are trying their level best for 
operationalizing all the DSPT sites. 
 

 
 
8

1.8.5 The Committee notes the effort made in ensuring mobile connectivity for CAPFs 
personnel posted in far flung/inaccessible areas and recommends Ministry to coordinate with 
DoT regularly and monitor the re-provisioning of DSPTs. 
 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.8.6 The Committee observes that just like Army Personnel, the CAPF personnel are also posted 
in the treacherous, mountainous and snowy terrains. Therefore, CAPFs personnel needs to be 
given the Risk and Hardship allowance as admissible to Army personnel. The Committee is of the 
opinion that parity on the payment of such allowances should be maintained between troops that are 
deployed in similar areas. This will go a long way in boosting the morale of the deployed CAPF 
personnel in tough condition and areas. 
(Para 4.3.18 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.8.7 Government has accepted recommendations of the 7th CPC for grant of Risk & Hardship 
Allowances to CAPF personnel at par with Defence Forces and orders were issued on 31.07.2017. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
1.8.8 The Committee is extremely happy that on the basis of its recommendation the 
Government has granted 'Risk and Hardship Allowances to CAPF' personnel at par with the 
Defence Forces which was also one of the recommendation of the 7th CPC. It will surely motivate 
of CAPF personnel who are posted at difficult terrains. 
 
 
1.9 Intelligence Bureau 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.9.1 The Committee notes that there are multiple agencies like IB, RAW, CAPFs, Army, State 
agencies, etc. in India which are collecting the intelligence inputs, This may be necessary keeping in 
view the size and political structure of the country. The biggest challenge, however, is how to 
coordinate, create and act upon the inputs/information gathered by these agencies. At times, due to 
lack of coordination, distrust amongst the intelligence agencies, timely action to prevent terrorist 
incidents could not be taken. Therefore, the Committee recommends that MHA should act as the focal 
point to coordinate amongst those intelligence agencies; device mechanism for collating intelligence 
inputs and sharing it on real-time basis through Multi- Agency Centre (MAC) to avoid any delay in 
taking necessary action on the ground level. The Committee further recommends for developing an 
effective mechanism to conduct validity checks on information obtained by the MAC from other 
agencies. As we are living in a globalized world which is inter-connected and inter-dependent, our 
intelligence agencies should strive for increased coordination and cooperation not only at District, 
State and Regional level but also at International level with friendly foreign counterparts in developing 
and sharing intelligence to mitigate and nullify threats.

Action Taken 
 
1.9.2 Introduction: The Multi-Agency Centre (MAC) was created in December 2001 in the 
aftermath of the Kargil Conflict as a platform  to  share, collate  and analyze all intelligence 
relating to terrorism. It was strengthened in December 2008 following 26/11 Mumbai terror attack. 
The  forum,  along with its Subsidiary MAC (SMAC) units in all States, has emerged as the 
nationally recognised coordinating agency for intelligence on terrorism and insurgency. A 
dedicated, secure electronic network for real-time sharing has been extended across the country, 
with two custom-built software platforms (TMS and NMB) for sharing and databasing intelligence. 
 
1.9.3 MAC-SMAC Connectivity: MAC has established a comprehensive system  of communication 
and connectivity to share/disseminate terrorism related information/data. For this purpose, the 
national capital was connected with 25 Central member agencies and all State capitals. In the 
State capitals, the network links the SMAC (housed in the Subsidiary Intelligence Bureau/SIB), 
State Police Special Branch, and offices of all central and other counter-terror agencies. 
Accordingly, a total of 374 locations are presently on the network.  In phase III, the network is 
being extended to 475 districts selected in consultation with State police chiefs. Out of 475 
identified locations, 451 locations have been found feasible for providing connectivity, out of which 
174 districts have already been connected. When completed, the network will cover 825 locations 
around the country. 
 
(i) The network hosts two software platforms: an intelligence sharing tool called Threat 
Management system (TMS) and a database tool called National Memory Bank (NMB). TMS 
was developed in-house by technical staff from IB, while the NMB software was developed 
by C- DAC, Pune on specifications provided by IB. 
(ii) NMB software is deployed on all MAC and State Police servers. A large amount of data has 
already been uploaded onto the database by IB and some other agencies including some of 
the States. 
 
1.9.4 Intelligence Sharing: On an average, every day MAC gathers, collates, stores, shares and 
disseminates about 150 inputs to concerned agencies. Special alerts are also issued as and when 
called for. The inputs are broadly divided under four heads - J&K, North-East, Left Wing Extremism 
and Rest of India. LWE- related inputs form the largest proportion of total inputs received by MAC 
currently, reflecting the spread of the problem across several States. 
 
1.9.5 Meetings: Various meetings are held regularly across the country to bring together all 
concerned agencies. 
 
1.9.6 A daily meeting of Nodal Officers from each member agency of MAC is held every day at 
MAC Headquarters to review inputs. MAC also conducts some specialized meetings: 
 
(i) Monthly meeting on Cross-Border Terrorism in J&K. 
(ii) Monthly meeting on insurgent camps, FICN and other anti-India activities in 
Bangladesh and Myanmar. 
Fortnightly meeting on LWE introduced in 2012. 
(iii) Monthly meeting on Sikh militancy in Punjab started in 2015. 
(iv) Focus Group Meetings on sensitive inputs received from various agencies/ channels. 
 
1.9.7 Intelligence Sharing with neighbouring countries: Gol has designated MAC as the nodal 
point for sharing of intelligence with Bangladesh and Myanmar. In this capacity, inputs on 
terrorism are regularly shared with counterparts in these countries.

1.10 Central Police Organizations 
 
Recommendation 
 
1.10.1 The Committee notes the increase in drug seizure for the past three years. But this has not 
decreased illicit trafficking of narcotics. Moreover, with the increasing popularity of crypto-currencies, 
"darknet" markets have grown where drug traffickers are using encryption software to protect their 
communications, data and money which makes it difficult to track and seize drugs. Therefore, the 
Committee strongly recommends that efforts should be made to take effective measures against the 
Dark Net and ToR kind of software. Further, critical analysis of intelligence inputs on drug trafficking 
routes should also be done and officers of the NCB should be imparted requisite knowledge and skills 
through befitting training to prevent, investigate and disrupt drug trafficking. The Committee observes 
that as the types of drugs trafficked and the routes used are constantly evolving, it is essential to 
develop cooperation and information-sharing mechanism between regional, national and international 
law enforcement agencies. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the NCB should be 
provided with sufficient and sophisticated infrastructures, personnel, and coordinated enforcement 
mechanisms to combat the growing and fast-changing activities of drug traffickers especially on the 
International Borders. 
(Para 4.8.9 ibid) 
Action Taken 
 
1.10.2 The drug traffickers are increasingly using the Dark Net for trafficking in drugs. The medium 
offers complete anonymity because of the use of onion routing, use of Crypto Currency for payment 
and PGP encryption. NCB’s expertise and capacity to deal with this need to be augmented. 
Nonetheless, with available resources the NCB arrested a Dark Net vendor who was operating as an 
active vendor   of   Psychotropic   Drug   in   Dark   Net   markets.   This   network  had international 
linkages spread across India, Singapore and USA. During the operation, approximately 135 Kg of 
different Psychotropic tablets were seizedand 4 persons were arrested. 
 
1.10.3 Keeping in view the constant changing pattern of Drug trafficking and its abuse and the need 
to develop skills of Officers to respond to the challenges arising out of the same, this Ministry has, in 
December, 2019 set up A Training Centre on Drug Law Enforcement within the campus of the 
Central Academy of Police Training, Bhopal. This institute is mandated to impart domain training to 
the Officers of NCB and those of other Central and State Agencies involved in drug law enforcement. 
 
1.10.4 For the purpose of Coordination among all States/Central Agencies in drug related issues, a 
Narco Coordination mechanism was set up by MHA in 2016 under the chairmanship of DG (NCB).

more effective platform, the mechanism has been revamped in July, 2019 into a four tier structure- (1) 
Apex Committee headed by Union Home Secretary (2) Executive Committee headed by SS(Internal

Security) (3) State level Committee headed by Chief Secretary, (4) District Level Committee headed

1.10.5 For cooperation and information-sharing at international level, the NCB has entered into

bring foreign exchange to Lakshadweep. However, reckless and unsystematic growth may prove to be
